items.title: Roy Carew Interview, 1958-Fall
items.q: Clarence Williams had published, claimed it, in 1923 about... I never heard Tony play it... He used to kid about or laugh about Clarence.

ctx.x: Yeah, that's right, Charles. That's right. Well, he also, I talked to him, the last time I saw him was in New York, and he played the test pressings of those things just before they were issued. And he said that he didn't like the way he did Michigan Water. They insisted he do it that way, and he didn't want to do it that way. And I don't know what he had in mind.

Well, I'll say this about Michigan Water. Clarence Williams had published, claimed it, in 1923 about. Whereas, according to John Lewis, Tony was playing that thing years before that. And as far as the tune itself goes, the verse, I had heard it before that thing, considerably. And I think maybe they got the music of Clarence Williams, and had him follow that to a certain extent, because in a way he does follow, not too closely. But Clarence Williams doubtless picked it up from Tony or from somebody else around…

Well, you know, I think that the much more talented composer than Clarence was the... Oh, that other one. Spencer. Spencer, yeah. Yeah, he was. Spencer was a beautiful thing. Well, Spencer was a pretty well-known piano player in New Orleans too, wasn't he?

items.title: Roy Carew Interview, 1961-06-21
items.q: he went up there and he asked clarence williams he says i think i can get clarence williams to to act as agent for us on this i said all right it's all right with me so he got clarence and they went over to robert teller sons and donor the publishers

ctx.x: collected dimes on corners or something of that sort. In Chicago in later years they'd go from tavern to tavern. Singers are small instrumental groups, and today you can hear them on Halstead Street and some of the places where there are open air markets. Set up a loudspeaker and a guitar. The one thing I remember

close to that is that at the corner Canal and Rampart Street there used to be a small open truck, one of these light delivery trucks with an open wagon. And they had a couple of pieces of music in that, and a Negro standing in the back or sitting in the back singing. They used to give a little concert there on the street like that, but it wasn't like a street singer really. It wasn't Clarence Williams and Pirone trying to sell their music for us. No, I never saw them. The messenger at the Custom House when I was…
Well, I have seen the cover. Have you? Yes. Someone in Chicago has a copy of it, and I think I've seen your... Is that Mr. Hardin or someone by the name? Yes, yes. You know him? Yes.
